title: 3 John
subtitle: a note to a generous host, about traveling brothers and a man who loves to be first
lead: 3 John is a private letter from "the Elder" to his friend Gaius, so short that A. E. Brooke thought it was written to fit on one sheet of papyrus. It is the shortest book of the New Testament in Greek words, and the only one that never names Jesus or Christ. The Elder thanks Gaius for receiving traveling brothers, strangers to him, who went out "for the sake of the Name," and asks him to send them on their journey in a way worthy of God.

Then he names a problem. In another church, Diotrephes, "who loves to be first," has refused the Elder's letter and his people, and drives out of the church anyone who receives them. Gaius is told to imitate the good, not the bad, and is given a good example in Demetrius. The letter is a window on the first churches: missionaries on the road, hosts who fed them, letters of recommendation, and a quarrel over who could shut a church's door.
facts: "The Elder" (1:1), the writer of 2 John; traditionally John the apostle. See 2 John for the views.
Uncertain; written about the same time as 2 John (the endings are almost the same). Proposals run from the 60s to about AD 110.
House churches linked by traveling missionaries, in tradition around Ephesus in the Roman province of Asia
A private letter, in part a letter of recommendation for Demetrius
Greek, plain and close to 2 John

1 chapter, 14 verses in the KJV numbering this site uses; 15 in the SBL Greek text, which makes the last sentences of 1:14 a verse 15. 219 words in the SBL Greek text, the fewest of any New Testament book.
Gaius, Diotrephes and Demetrius, known only from this letter
authorship: The apostle John, writing as "the Elder" late in life, to a friend in one of the churches of Asia. The same writer as 2 John, by the title, the opening line and the nearly identical ending.

Eusebius listed 2 and 3 John among the disputed books, unsure "whether they belong to the evangelist or to another person of the same name," and Jerome reports that many gave them to John the presbyter, whom Papias had named. Some scholars today identify the writer with this John or with another leader of the Johannine circle.

Most scholars agree that the writer of 2 John wrote 3 John; a minority doubt it. Plummer, who held the apostle's authorship, granted that Diotrephes' treatment of the writer is the strongest point against it. Rudolf Bultmann held that 2 John was a forgery based on 3 John. C. H. Dodd counted the significant words: about 30 percent of those in 3 John do not appear in 1 John or the Gospel, against about 20 percent for 2 John.

audience.to: Gaius, a believer able to host and supply traveling Christians, probably brought to faith by the Elder ("my own children," 1:4), and apparently a member of a church other than Diotrephes'. The letter is personal ("you" singular throughout), but it also concerns the "friends" around Gaius (1:14).
audience.why: Traveling brothers sent out by the Elder's circle had been well received by Gaius, but turned away by Diotrephes, who refused the Elder's letter and expelled those who welcomed the brothers. The Elder writes to thank Gaius, to ask him to go on supporting the mission, to warn him about Diotrephes, and to recommend Demetrius, who probably carried the letter. Knowing this changes the reading: the letter is not a doctrinal tract but a working note in a network of house churches, and verse 2 is a friend's greeting, not a promise to every believer.
views: The Elder has to tell Gaius what Diotrephes is doing, and speaks of Diotrephes' church as "them" (C. H. Dodd on the first point; the NET Bible's note on 3 John 9 on the second).
Gaius belongs to the same church and is one of those Diotrephes threatens to expel (a suggestion the NET Bible's note on 3 John 9 mentions and rejects).

outline: Greeting to Gaius; the wish for his health; joy at children walking in the truth
Praise for his welcome to traveling brothers; send them on in a way worthy of God
Diotrephes, who loves to be first, refuses the Elder and his people
A visit soon; peace and greetings, each by name

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads the letter in its world: Christian travelers who relied on hosts, letters of recommendation like the papyrus of Theon for his brother Heraclides (about AD 25), the ordinary health wish of a Greek letter, and the Didache's rules for testing travelers.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks the scholars' questions: the writer and his relation to 2 John, who Diotrephes was (Harnack's early bishop, a rival host, a theological opponent), whether the refused letter is 2 John, the date, the variants, and why so short a letter was nearly left out of the canon.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Reads the private letter's craft: the health wish turned into a prayer, the contrasts of Gaius and Diotrephes, receiving and refusing, good and bad, and the key words truth, testimony and beloved.

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads the letter beside Jewish hospitality (Abraham's tent, "Let your house be open wide"), "the Name" as the Jewish way of speaking of God's name, and the greeting of peace, shalom.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: Reads with the church: the later traditions about Gaius and Demetrius as bishops, Diotrephes as the picture of a proud church leader, the debate over church order, and 3 John 2 in the prosperity teaching and its critics.

sections.b:
Read it as a real letter, carried by hand from one house church to another, probably by Demetrius. Then read 2 John beside it. The two share their writer, their opening ("whom I love in truth") and their ending ("I had a lot to write to you... face to face"). In 2 John the Elder tells a church not to take in teachers who deny the truth; in 3 John he praises Gaius for taking in the Elder's own messengers, and complains of Diotrephes, who shut them out. Together they show the door of a house church as the place where the early Christian movement was kept or blocked.

The notes mark the places where English hides the Greek: "in every way" and "doing well" in 1:2 (the KJV's "above all things... prosper"), "strangers at that" (1:5), "the Name" (1:7), "who loves to be first" (1:9) and the friends greeted "each by name" (1:14).

The KJV ends 3 John at verse 14, and so do the site's verse keys and the English versions it checks. The SBL Greek text makes the last three short sentences ("Peace to you. The friends send you greetings. Greet each of the friends by name") a separate verse 15. The Plain English Translation prints them under 1:14, with a note. Nothing is added or missing; only the counting differs, so a reader using a Bible with fifteen verses will find the same words.

sections.h: 3 John among the books of the Bible
sections.b: 3 John was the least quoted of the three letters, probably because it is so short and private. The earliest clear mentions come in the middle of the 200s: Eusebius reports that Origen knew of "perhaps also a second and third" letter of John, "but not all consider them genuine" (Church History 6.25.10), and that Origen's pupil Dionysius of Alexandria spoke of "the reputed second or third epistle of John" (7.25.11). Eusebius himself, about 325, counted 2 and 3 John among the disputed writings "which are nevertheless recognized by many" (3.25.3). Athanasius' Easter letter of 367, the Synod of Hippo and the Council of Carthage (397) list all three letters. The Syriac Peshitta left out 2 and 3 John until the Harklean version of 616. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Bibles today include the letter, though current Lutheran usage still counts it among the "antilegomena," the once-disputed books. See 2 John for the fuller story and the topic page on the canon.

The text of 3 John is well preserved, and the differences between manuscripts are small (A. E. Brooke). The site follows NA28, whose text in these letters is the Editio Critica Maior's; in 3 John it differs from the SBL text only at 1:4, where NA28 has no article ("walking in truth"). The variants worth knowing are where the KJV differs: "for his name's sake" (1:7, KJV), "to the brethren, and to strangers" (1:5, KJV), "receive such" (1:8, KJV), "I wrote unto the church" without "something" (1:9, KJV), and "Our friends" (1:14, KJV), where "Our" is not in the Greek.

spec.title: Claude's theory: a letter of recommendation in disguise
spec.body: This is my own reading, building on Dodd's and Plummer's suggestion that Demetrius carried the letter. If so, the whole letter is shaped toward 1:12. The Elder first praises Gaius for receiving strangers (1:5-8), then shows what refusing them looks like (1:9-10), then states the principle, "imitate the good" (1:11), and only then names the man at the door. The papyrus letter of Theon for his brother (about AD 25) asks its reader to treat the bearer as one recommended; 3 John asks the same, but builds the case first, so that Gaius, faced with Demetrius, can only choose to act like himself and not like Diotrephes. The order of the argument is my observation; the identification of Demetrius as the bearer is Plummer's and Dodd's.

prompts: The traveling brothers at Gaius' door

A hand-drawn scroll scene in ink and earth colors: a courtyard of a modest Roman-era house in Asia Minor at dusk, a host in a plain tunic welcoming three dusty travelers with staffs and bags, a woman bringing bread and a water jar, a small oil lamp in the doorway. Mixed style of ancient manuscript drawing, cave-art figures and modern line art, soft torn parchment edges, no hard rectangle.

A sketch on aged papyrus: a heavy wooden door of a house church, half shut, a stern man in a good cloak standing in it with his arm across the opening, travelers turning away down a road toward a distant figure holding a small letter. Loose ink lines, ochre wash, faded edges.

A playful cave-drawing style panel: a reed pen, an ink pot and a single small sheet of papyrus with a few lines of Greek, the word EIRENE (peace) at the bottom, framed by a ring of small stick figures with names above their heads. Earth tones, soft irregular border.
